This mystical understanding of Adam—the manifestation of God in the heavenly human form, itself the manifestation of God’s essential attribute of beauty—gives rise to a corresponding understanding of prophecy. Prophecy, too, is understood through the revelation of the divine in human beauty. The importance of this theme cannot be overstated.

By presenting Muhammad as the prophet of the religion of mystical love, it shows how Sufism understands itself: as a mystical religion that discloses the inner meaning of prophetic religion. The Prophet as he lives in the consciousness of Sufism—a young Arab “in love with his God”—is quite different from the figure usually presented by the historical study of religions.

But we are not concerned here with historical criticism. We are describing the structure of a spiritual experience. For the Sufis, Muhammad is the prophet of the divine assumption of human form, the revelation of divine beauty in the beauty of the human form. This was his distinctive prophetic gift, setting him apart from all the prophets before him. He testified to it both in inspired sayings that echo the verses of the Book revealed through the Angel and in his own visionary experience, which, together with his prophetic calling, makes him the model of mystical experience for the Sufi.
Among the sayings that have given Sufis inexhaustible material for meditation is one that bears witness to the Imago Dei, the divine image.

We must give it its full force. It speaks of an image whose visible shape corresponds to the invisible divine reality: the Form of God (sûrat al-Haqq) to which the Prophet himself testified when he told of seeing his God “in the most beautiful of forms.” This resemblance, this meeting of the two, is not a result of the divine Act; it is that Act, the act of divine self-manifestation.

“The whole substance of Adam’s being was poured into the mould of the theophany.” Similarly, the other hadith in which God declares that, when his faithful servant draws close to him, God himself becomes that servant’s sight, hearing, hand, and so on, already applies to Adam. We have encountered this archetype of mystical union (unio mystica) arising in the very first theophany.

When the Prophet, bringing together the threefold initiative of religious Law (sharî’at), the spiritual Path (tarîqat), and mystical Truth (haqîqat), “saw with the eyes of the soul the imprint of the Beloved in the mirror formed by Adam’s very substance, he proclaimed to the holy Spirits (arwâh-e qodsî, the spiritual individualities of human beings), in a voice of triumph: God created Adam in the image of his own form.”

Muhammad thus takes on the role of the archangel Michael, calling the angels to adore the human form—that is, divine humanity, the purest substance of their own heavenly realm. The heavenly Adam was their shâhid, their witness of contemplation. They knew that this did not contradict the declaration that “nothing resembles Him,” and that, conversely, to deny every resemblance in order to avoid tashbîh (likening God to created things) is to fall into the emptiness of abstraction (ta’til, stripping God of meaningful attributes).

“The Light of divinity rose first upon that Niche of Lights (meshkat) which is the form of Adam; from there its Sun rose over all the witnesses of contemplation who make its beauty present … All things and beings that have received some of this light are, in this world and for the Faithful in Love, flowers in the garden of the one Beauty and Majesty.”

“The nearer one is to the source of beauty, the nearer one is to the covenant of love.” That is why the Prophet, with a “gesture of feminine tenderness,” would hasten to kiss and lift to his eyes anything in this world that had freshly blossomed forth from the Beloved. Whenever he saw a rose, he would raise it to his eyes and say: “The red rose belongs to the beauty of God!” Such, for him, was the privilege of every beautiful being.

“Whoever has been granted beauty has been chosen by the divine light, singled out for the sweetness of intimacy; such a one is called a second Adam.” And so the other famous saying follows naturally: “God is beautiful and loves beauty.” The beauty he loves is his own beauty, which he shows to himself in the form of Adam.

This is why the Prophet’s saying points both to the beauty of Adam as shâhid, the witness of contemplation, and to the beauty of Paradise as mashhad, the place where this witness makes the beauty of the primordial divine contemplation present. For this is what Paradise is: “Every being whose beauty we admire bears the trace of this twofold beauty—that of the shâhid and that of the mashhad, of Adam and of Paradise.”
Paradise, then, is wherever beauty bears witness to, and makes present, the identity of love, lover, and beloved. In turn, that identity is reflected in another: love, Paradise, and beauty are one.

Thus the Prophet affirmed that “the supreme Good toward which beings aspire in this world and the next appears to every human being in the features of lover and beloved. For the love between lover and beloved is the direct influence (ta’thîr) of the love inherent in the divine realities (ilâhîyât).” The force that moves the lover is therefore a love that existed before all time. Beauty is the “phenomenon of the divine,” the divine appearing that sets this love alight. Beauty bears the divine lights in its twofold nature, and leads whoever loves it back to the very Source of those lights.
In a third saying, the prophet of divine Beauty gives the Faithful in Love their rule: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies keeping the secret of that love, dies as a true witness.”

Another saying alludes to the eternal foundation of this rule: “Concerning the pre-eminence of the Faithful in Love, there is a subtle allusion which can serve beginners as a sign guiding them along the path of love, while for those who have attained perfection it is a symbolic account of love’s origins.”

This “subtle allusion,” this “symbolic account,” will be developed below (theme 4). It concerns the existence of the holy Spirits—the spiritual individualities of human beings—before their earthly lives, a theme in which Platonic memories grow into a prophetic philosophy of love.

As for “dying of love,” we must understand it, first, in the literal sense of physical death, brought about by a passion so overwhelming that it engulfs the whole person. This presupposes a human constitution in which psychic energies exert all the greater force because unconscious life has not yet been restrained by the rational organization of existence or by the demands and prohibitions of a complex society. The physical organism is then less protected; the soul’s upheavals are felt, and their effects resound, with their full intensity.

A deep belief in the eternity of Spirits is itself a sign of a cultural world in which the relations between psyche and body are experienced quite differently from societies dominated by agnosticism and rationalism. That death from love must also be taken “literally” is suggested by the stories of certain famous heroes of ‘Udhrî love, as well as by those gatherings of mystical preaching in which merely speaking of the Eternal Bride could cause a number of listeners to fall unconscious.

But “dying of love” must also be understood as a mystical death. Here it means the complete burning away of the desires of the carnal soul, the very thing the Prophet calls the chastity of love. When the soul has been entirely consumed and the fire dies down, the soul has kept its secret. It is now ready for the transformation in which the contemplator becomes the contemplated, and the lover the beloved, for the gaze with which the soul looks is the very gaze of the face it beholds; and that face, in turn, beholds the soul that looks upon it.

At the end of this chapter (theme 6), we shall see that this was the case with Majnûn, and that it distinguishes him from the heroes of ‘Udhrî love generally. When Majnûn’s original ego has been so completely consumed that he can speak as Layla in the first person, he becomes the pure image of esoteric tawhîd, the innermost truth of divine oneness.

To reach it, one must undergo the “mystical death of love.” The witness of contemplation is no longer merely a shâhid, but a shahîd: a true witness, a “martyr”. This is the degree of love the Prophet meant in his saying.

The lover who attains such faithfulness becomes a companion of the prophets, because Beauty itself has a prophetic function above all others: it is Beauty to which the “witnesses” testify, Beauty which they make present and bring into contemplation. The Hurufis would later stress this idea: the Qur’an is a silent book, while the beauty of the human face is a speaking Qur’an. Both therefore call for a prophetic interpretation.
But every ta’wîl, every uncovering of an inner meaning, is also an interpretation of the soul—an exodus in which the soul returns to the true meaning.

To pass through the “true meaning” of beauty is to undergo this mystical death, which raises the faithful lover to the rank of true witness, shahîd, and prophet, Nabî: “When love has raised the lover to the rank of true Witness (shahîd), he becomes the companion of the prophets in the world of Jabarût [divine power] and the fields of Malakût [the angelic realm], riding with them upon love’s mount, for the royal road of love is the place (mashâhid) where martyrs are slain and prophets bear witness.”

It was upon this Path, where prophets and faithful lovers share the same witness and the same prophetic contemplation, that Muhammad encountered the mystery of theophany in a form suited to him. The account is among the most famous and cherished of all hadith for the Sufis.

Rûzbehân writes: “The light that rises upon the visible form of a beloved being is the light of archetypal divine beauty. The beloved, invested with these qualities, derives them from God, for it is the Sun of Majesty that rises upon that face from the height of the mountain before all time. If you have the eyes to see, contemplate how this Sun rises over a beloved face.

“In the mirror formed by the delicate substance of its visible shape, contemplate the light of the star that is its soul. See how that star rises in the East formed by the visible expression of its qualities, and lights up the entire universe of that person.” Whoever understands this can begin to penetrate the secret of beauty’s twofold significance.

Archetypal beauty appeared to the Prophet in a face that served as his shâhid, his witness of contemplation; yet he realized that he himself was also the shâhid: the one who sees and is seen. Whether we say that an outward form was perceived in the visionary state as a theophany, or that a form inwardly perceived in vision appeared with all the objective, mind-independent reality of a visible form, is a difference of interpretation. What remains is the Prophet’s testimony in the extraordinary hadith of the vision: “I saw my Lord in the most beautiful of forms.”

This testimony is invoked again and again in Rûzbehân’s Jasmine. It can indeed be regarded as the central pillar of the theophanic religion of the Faithful in Love. It stands equally far from tashbîh, the crude likening of God to created things, and ta’til, the emptying of God of every attribute. It resolves the difficulties of tanzîh, the insistence that God is beyond all resemblance, through a perception arising at a level unknown to abstract monotheism.

During this theophany, the Prophet “asked for the love without whose sweetness he could imagine no sweetness in the world. He said: I ask You for Your love, the love of everyone who loves You, and the love of a deed that brings me nearer to Your love. Through the beautiful witness of contemplation [the Youth seen in the vision], eternal Beauty had broken into his soul; and now, beneath the overwhelming power of that vision’s beauty, pure love blossomed in him.”

Muhammad was thus the prophet of divine Eros. By announcing that “He created the human being in the image of his own form,” he showed himself capable of enduring the shock of the divine appearance: the theophany in the radiance of human beauty. He testified that he had truly seen this vision “in the most beautiful of forms.”

The hadith of the vision sounds like a paradoxical answer to the refusal given to Moses: “You shall not see Me (lan tarânî).” The mountain from whose summit Moses asked God, “Show Yourself to me,” was, according to Rûzbehân, the mountain of Moses’ own being. “Look at the mountain,” he was told.

But when God manifested himself to it, the mountain was shattered, and Moses fell unconscious. Muhammad was the first to bear the shock of this theophany. This also distinguishes him, as the prophet of visionary love for divine Beauty, from Abraham, the hero of faith. Scattered through several pages of the Jasmine are subtle teachings on the matter, all affirming the pre-eminence of human beauty over every other kind of beauty.

Abraham entered the path of the malakût through the “openings” of the divine Act—that is, the manifestations of divinity visible to the eye of astrology, the heavenly bodies. In the event that led to his prophetic calling, he directed his vision toward the Signs (âyât) themselves.

Thus, in the urgency of his search and the force of his longing, he exclaimed, “This is my Lord” (Qur’an 6:76–78). It follows that if the Eternal Bride had shown herself to him, as she did to Muhammad, in the form of human beauty, what befell Moses would have befallen Abraham at this stage of his search. For in the mirror of the cosmos God appears through the attributes of Sublimity and Power, whose onslaught breaks the harmony of contemplative knowledge.

Abraham awoke to consciousness of the invisible malakût and freed himself from the wandering stars of the heavens. The “three that set” (Sun, Moon, and Venus) are manifestations of the Signs (majâlî-e âyât); they are the place of faith. They are not, as human beauty is, the manifestation of the Essence (majâlî-e dhât)—the divine assumption of human form, the “place” of direct vision.

But Abraham’s “turn” (nawbat) had not yet come to behold human beauty. The turn of such direct vision was reserved for the one who would be the Seal of the Prophets. Therefore, realizing that direct vision of eternal archetypal Beauty was not to be found among the Signs (the marvels in the heavens), Abraham withdrew toward his Lord (37:97). Becoming a stranger to all else and rediscovering himself in the beauty of his own soul, he chose the mirror of the heart over the visible Signs, for in that mirror he saw God with the eyes of his innermost consciousness.

Abraham was content to see what is hidden—the invisible reality of God (ma’nâ-ye Haqq)—with the eye of that innermost consciousness. The time had not yet come to “contemplate the eternal Face of God in the mirror offered by the eyes of human lovers.” After the prophet who was the hero of faith, the prophet announcing love still had to come. Through him the prophetic meaning of human Beauty would blossom, raising its witness to the rank of a prophet.

Rûzbehân has much to say about this point, so decisive for the Faithful in Love and their understanding of prophecy: “As for the difference between human beauty and beauty other than the human kind—the beauty of colours and things in this world—it is that human beauty is privileged to bear the lights of the theophany of the Essence (anewâr-e tajallî-e dhât), whereas other things owe their beauty to the freshness of a newly blossoming divine manifestation (tarâwat-e f’l).

“Contemplation of the cosmos is the qibla [direction of devotion] of the pious; contemplation of human beauty is the qibla of the Faithful in Love. The powerless defenders of religious conformity criticize us. The Signs of creation in the heavens are more sublime, they say. Why do you not contemplate them? Certainly there are Signs (âyât) in the heavens, and they show the way to inconsolable hearts.

“But upon the human face rises the sun of the theophany of the divine Essence and Attributes. For it was through human beauty that love entered this world, while faith entered it through the body of the cosmos. Whoever has entered the state of love (‘âshiq) no longer looks at the outer world; the only event he sees in the world is what appears upon Joseph’s beautiful face. Love and beauty spring from the same mine: the divine Attributes … To love beauty is to see eternal existence with the very eye of God.”

Whether human love experiences beauty as a theophany—or, in other words, experiences itself as the consciousness through which beauty is revealed as a theophany—depends on awakening to this hidden meaning within the twofold nature of what the senses perceive. Here Rûzbehân continues his “phenomenology” of spiritual experience, examining the lived state in which the phenomenon of beauty becomes manifest.

The spiritual state that allows beauty to appear, that serves as the organ through which it is perceived, and on which its character as a theophany depends—the “divine eye” contemplating itself—is essentially love. A phenomenology of beauty is a phenomenology of love. Beauty reveals its prophetic meaning to the perfected lover, who has become a companion of the prophets.

Rûzbehân identifies four elements or “pillars” (arkân) of love’s first appearance. (a) The lover’s inmost nature must have become wholly spiritual. The lover must have learned to distinguish the soul’s nature from physical nature and have acquired the capacity to join with purely spiritual beings. (b) The veil hiding the soul is then lifted.

Through its inward powers of seeing and perceiving, the soul joins with the light of the pure beings of the malakût; and their light is the very source and archetype of beauty. (c) Through the meeting of these two lights, the soul has become a pure mirror, a mazhar, a place where the divine appears. It has become akin to love itself and taken on love’s colour (ham-rang, yak-rang: of one colour, perfectly one in hue).

Until now, its capacity was still wholly undetermined. Now, corresponding to that capacity, there is a particular form through which Beauty can appear to the soul, be recognized by it, and be invested with the character of the beloved (ma’shûq). (d) The form of beauty corresponding to the form of love for which this heart has the capacity had so far existed only as a possibility, not yet as an event. “When the light of uncreated Beauty rises out of the fine mist and shines upon the beauty of a lovely creature, archetypal Beauty at last presents itself face to face before the lover’s eyes.”

These two lights—the light of archetypal Beauty shining through the beloved’s beauty and the light present in the lover’s gaze—appear outwardly to be two separate realities. In their true being, however, they form a single whole expressed in two inseparable and mutually dependent conditions: that of the lover (‘âshiq), whose presence makes possible the perception of beauty and the recognition of the beloved as beloved; and that of the beloved (ma’shûq), whose presence makes possible the lover’s condition as lover. This is why their respective qualities—the capacity of the one and the beauty of the other—are intimately attuned.

Here, too, there is a twofold meaning, an ambiguity that belongs to the experience itself: the one who contemplates becomes the one contemplated, and the lover sees his own face in the beloved, because the light of his gaze and the light of that beauty are, in reality, two aspects of one light. The beloved’s qualities—that is, the invisible spiritual attributes hidden within the beloved’s capacity to be loved (ma’shûqîya), through which the beloved holds sway over the lover—are made manifest through beauty by means of the lover’s active imagination. Inner and outer realities are perfectly synchronized.

What occurs here corresponds to the indivisible relationship between rabb and marbûb: the personal Lord and the person devoted to that Lord. This is a radical freeing of the relationship from its social and collective framework, unlike the relation generally envisaged by outward-looking theologies between God as universal ruler and humanity as a whole.

Here lies the prophetic meaning of beauty. As the beloved, without even knowing it, comes to exercise the lordly power conferred by beauty, the God who is love reveals himself both to himself and to the world. This revelation takes the form of a power so foreign to every attempt to turn the divine into a collective institution that it brings such attempts to an end. The beloved’s power thus reveals the true nature of the “victorious,” royal authority belonging to the divine condition of lordship.

In relation to the servant of love, the beloved is God and Lord (rabb); yet this rabb, this personal Lord, could not continue to exist for even an instant without the faithful lover. In other words, the secret of robûbîya, the divine lordship of the personal Lord loved by the mystic, and the secret of ma’shûqîya, the beloved’s condition of being invested with lordly power, are one and the same secret: an eternal companionship.

And in that companionship, as Rûzbehân’s anonymous commentator quietly suggests, even if power and authority belong to the beloved, perhaps the benefit and advantage belong to the lover in servitude, since the beloved’s very reign depends upon the lover’s service of love.
Now the four “pillars” (arkân), the four elements that constitute love, have been brought together. Love takes shape in the two persons of lover and beloved.

Yet all this, even taken together, still amounts only to love in an imperfect, figurative sense (majâzî), not love in its full reality. An inner pilgrimage must now begin. Its success will determine whether the lover reaches real love, love in its true sense (haqîqî): the awareness that the beauty he loves is a theophany, and that it is not despite its twofold character but because of it that beauty can lead him toward the reality it reveals. In other words, it falls to the lover to bring the prophetic meaning of beauty into flower. That is why, as love awakens, anguish and restlessness awaken in the lover’s heart as well.

The intellect remains captivated by the ambiguity inherent in love awakened by a beautiful human face. The spirit (rûh) turns away from the direct vision of the true Beloved, whom the beauty of the shâhid, its witness of contemplation, makes present to it.

To recover that vision, it must keep watch through the openings of the five senses, attaining through each organ of sense perception the particular theophany proper to it. This is love’s twofold nature, and why the lover must pass through every experience of human love as through stages of an ascent, until their fullness is attained: “direct vision (shohûd) of the divine Face in a beautiful form offered to contemplation, in the person of a human creature with a beautiful face.”

But the pilgrimage is difficult and dangerous (its stages are described below, in theme 5). It holds severe suffering in store and demands a personal discipline sterner than any collective rules of morality or religious Law.

When the veil of human love (‘ishq insânî) that concealed divine love (‘ishq rabbânî) is lifted, the lover’s love becomes an initiate’s love, “not in the sense that his eyes close to the beloved’s outward, visible form or turn away from it, but in the sense that the lover now reaches an inward unveiling of love (kashf-e ‘ishq, an intuition that reveals love’s transcendent meaning, its haqîqat). It becomes clear to him that the Divine Being reveals itself to him in the beloved’s beauty [that is, he contemplates a theophany, tajallî, in that beauty]. He becomes aware of mysterious divine actions working upon him through the beloved’s form, even though the beloved’s visible form [the person who exists outwardly, independently of the lover] remains unaware of them.”

The beloved is invested with this theophanic function before even becoming aware of the capacity to fulfil it. For this to happen, the beloved must awaken to self-knowledge, must know herself as the lover knows her, as she exists in her Image—the very Image she herself presents to him as her shâhid, her witness of contemplation.

The prophetic meaning of beauty is then fulfilled within the very person entrusted with it, and there is “light upon light.” Something occurs, for example, like the conclusion of Rûzbehân’s experience in Mecca, which Ibn ‘Arabî recalls when he speaks of the beautiful singer’s “conversion.” This is also the conclusion toward which the Jasmine reaches as it offers itself to the woman to whom it is dedicated, inviting her to know herself as God contemplates himself within her.

Yet the rule is unyielding: “If the initiate has been purified of every sensual weakness in human love, he will stand firm in divine love [that is, the love through which human beauty is perceived as a theophany].
“But if any stain of carnal appetite remains upon the soul’s robe, then, in the world of divine love, the initiate will be thrown from the mount that carries love’s mystical reality (haqîqat).”

Whatever the dangers, the answer is not a harsh and negating monastic asceticism. If bodily love is the path leading toward spiritual love, it is because it arises from an alchemy older than time. “Although, from the standpoint of what is essential, bodily love is a lower stage, love is nevertheless the influence of the Red Sulphur of divine Magnificence, cast into the light of the soul’s eyes.

“Thus, from before all eternity, the alchemical work has hidden a soul within the soul of the soul.” This is why, in the two persons of lover and beloved, love is in truth one and the same tinctura, one colouring brought about by their unitive fusion (yak-rang: perfect oneness of colour). The mystical reality within love sounds a certain note, if you know how to listen.

Until you have tasted this drink—God! God!—you will understand nothing of our condition. Look into the garden of our love, and hear the singing birds give voice to “Glory be to me!” (the cry of Bastâmî) and “I am God!” (the cry of Hallâj). Listen to those melodies; hear how the minstrel plays the song of love.

There is a poignant urgency in this appeal from Rûzbehân to the beautiful being to whom his book is dedicated. He wants her to understand the light in which she stands, the theophanic vision he sees in and through her.

But the responsibility for revealing the prophetic meaning of her beauty to her rests upon the mystical lover himself. Should he falter, everything would be jeopardized. And the way is difficult. We have already heard Rûzbehân confess as much. “Since, by divine command, he had been able to contemplate only the veil of the Eternal Bride, he was veiled from the beloved [or rather, the beloved was veiled from him] by reason of the beloved herself.” He had first to undergo love’s ordeals and its madness, still without any clear understanding of himself.

He returns to this theme in an entire chapter. Speaking of himself in the third person, in the veiled language of personal confession, Rûzbehân takes up once again the four elements of love that he analysed earlier, now as a description of his own story. The passage is especially characteristic of his style: “This nightingale, this singer of a thousand songs, who suddenly fell into the net of the hunters of Trial, lured by the bait of vision, remained caught among the thorns of the rose garden: a certain moon-faced image.

“And there he is, the constant companion of the sufferings she inflicts upon him … Leaving the paradise of tranquillity, he came to the place where love humbles him to dust, though he brought with him love’s thousand prides … Among the pure-hearted Sufis in love’s retreats, he sings again the song of your gestures and washes with his tears the robe that his passion for you has dyed with the blood of love … Ask those who know the harsh law of anguish, those who read and reread the text of melancholy.

“Then you will learn the courage of this spiritual knight (javânmard, Rûzbehân) upon the Path of love, and discover who this sorrowing heart is among the kings of Knowledge … Oh, the wonder of this Phoenix, who turned from the heaven of everlastingness toward the world of annihilation, and from the world of annihilation turns again toward the world of everlastingness! See what kind of bird you have caught in your snare: the nest of the Sîmorgh of the Throne cannot hold the grain on which he feeds. The bride of Paradise asks God for nothing but his face.

“But look closely: in the heart of love lie all the caskets holding the mystery of the Face of Majesty, for the contemplation of a single hieroglyph in that heaven is enough to exchange angelic modesty for the exuberance of the lover’s condition.

“Then this faithful lover tears apart his heaven-coloured cloak [his Sufi cloak] and tastes the crumbs of the heavenly ones’ feast. Among the ranks of the Sufis, he proclaims the secret of Ego sum Deus (Anâ al-Haqq, ‘I am God’) … Who knows the cipher of this story except the Faithful in Love? Who can decipher the hieroglyphs of this way of being except the people of longing?”

For the pilgrimage of the faithful lover is governed by two concerns. The lover must meditate upon, uncover, and bring to life the prophetic meaning of beauty; and must remain alert to the danger of giving way to sensual desire. It is significant that among all the Iranian Faithful in Love, from Sanâ’î to Hâfez and beyond, every evocation of beauty’s prophetic meaning awakens memories of Zoroastrianism and finds expression in their distinctive “veiled language,” whose vocabulary is borrowed from the Mazdean tradition.

Whether in Sohrawardî or among the Sufis themselves, the religion of love brought forth the prophetic meaning of ancient Persia’s religion by transforming its technical terms into symbols (see Book II, chapter VI, section 3 above).

Thus Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Iran, came to be recognized as a prophet of that religion of love which Muhammad announced and to which he bore witness (see theme 2 above). Here Rûzbehân calls zand and pâzand—a choice his commentator particularly emphasizes—the spiritual interpretation of Beauty through which the soul also interprets itself and makes its own exodus from the regions ruled by the carnal soul. “At times, bowing down in love, he chants the zand and pâzand of love’s inspirations, reading them upon the tablet presented to him by the earthly image of the Eternal Bride’s beauty.

“At other times he must drive the pillagers, the ruffians of carnal nature, away from the place where his highest aspirations are gathered.” He must keep himself far from the shores of the transient, “and yet, within the darkness of nature in its elemental state, at the very source of the passions of the carnal soul, the gnostic, following in Khezr’s footsteps, drinks the Water of Life.” This is what the faithful lover finds hardest of all to make others understand: the very paradox of theophany, the presence within the world of the senses of a Presence that is not itself contained in that world.

“Although this pearl (the pearl of contemplation associated with the shâhid, the beautiful figure through whom the divine is contemplated) has the purity of a jewel, the hypocrites of legalistic religion and the small-minded devotees see in it a kind of incarnation. Great God! If those who have eyes fail to see, what will become of those who have none?

“Yet this is what was declared (by the Prophet) in an inspired saying: My friends are beneath my canopies; no one knows them but I. And the secret of the prophetic message has revealed that the Eternal Brides are kept in the bridal chambers of trial, hidden behind the veil of jealousy that has existed from before time. It is said: They look at you, yet they do not see you (7:197).
“Thus the beauty of this majesty, which throws the world of the soul into turmoil, is protected from the fury of those whose envy drives them to violence.”

The Qur’anic verse invoked here appears elsewhere in support of a kind of “docetism,” understood as a theological critique of appearances. It accords with the very rule governing our perception of divine manifestations, or theophanies: Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui—I saw him as I was capable of seeing him. Ruzbihan’s commentator explains this in turn through two famous verses.

The first is by Hafez: “Our idol appears before everyone's eyes; and yet the enchantment I behold is seen by no one but me.” Sa'di had already offered what might be called its answering verse: “Not every eye is fit to behold such beauty—only yours, for you draw around yourself the protecting circle of the divine Name.”

The development of the preceding theme led us to an allusion to an alchemical transformation accomplished before time began, the source of the mutual correspondence between lover and beloved. The idea that souls—the “holy Spirits”—recognize one another on earth because of a bond established in pre-eternity, before their earthly existence, is a favorite theme of this Sufism. It certainly recalls Plato. It also accords with the Zoroastrian belief in the preexistence of the fravartis before their descent to earth; and within Islam itself, Shiism explicitly professes the preexistence of souls. This is the “symbolic history” mentioned earlier, expressing the preeminence of those faithful to love.

We have already noted a distinctive feature of the religion of love professed by our Sufis: Muhammad is its prophet, but its language is one of Platonic symbols. In the Jasmine, this “prologue in heaven” to the earthly history of love takes two forms.

The first is simply Platonic. It is natural to encounter it here, just as we encounter it in Leone Ebreo’s Dialogues of Love. Ruzbihan, however, does not speak of the androgynous being. That idea does find a counterpart in his final conception of lover and beloved as two ways of being united in a single being. The other form of the story comes from the Qur’an. Seen from the outside, the connection between it and the event symbolized in the Platonic account may not be immediately obvious.

But the connection becomes clear as soon as we understand the relationship between human and divine love established in Ruzbihan's mystical teaching. We need not ask, as though faced with a contradiction: Since the holy Spirits knew one another before earthly existence, is it their companion they long to find again (the Platonic version)? Or is the one they long to find the Lord whom they acclaimed before time began (the Qur’anic version)? There is no dilemma.

Human love initiates us into the secret of divine love, which brings it to perfection; in finding their companion again, the Spirits find their Lord. More precisely, the passage from one kind of love to the other does not mean transferring love from one object to another. This is what esoteric tawhîd, the inner meaning of divine oneness, will reveal.

Ruzbihan presents the first version of the story in these words, following the Prophet's saying that alludes to it: “The religion of love grounds human love in this sacred symbol. It knows that in their homeland, in the high city of God, the holy Spirits gazed upon one another when they dwelt within the canopies (sarâdiq) of the divine Presence. As they contemplated one another, they saw the traces of God that permeated their being. Moved by this beauty, they joined together, each drawn to others according to the degree of their affinity.

“When they came into this world, they looked at one another again with those same eyes, according to their prevailing capacity, the purity of their being, the understanding possessed by each intelligence, and the nearness of soul to soul. In one another's faces they recognized each other and came to love one another. As our Prophet said: The Spirits are like troops gathered together; those who recognize each other form bonds of mutual affection, while those who do not recognize each other remain at odds.”

Here, then, is the second version of this symbolic history. It appears in the chapter devoted specifically to mystical love, understood in terms of three modes or degrees of vision among contemplatives capable of visionary perception (ahl-e moshâhadat). The central figure in this scene “in heaven” is the Eternal Witness of Contemplation (shâhid-e qidam).

Here the relationship between the Eternal Witness and the shâhid in the ordinary sense—the human beauty that manifests the divine and makes it present in the mystic's heart—comes into sharper focus. It cannot be resolved by treating them as two objects standing in relation to one another. It can be understood only through a transformation in the seer's own vision, precisely the subject of this chapter.

In such a transformed vision, the shâhid appears to human love in such a way that it is God himself who looks upon this shâhid, and who looks upon himself through it. To understand what a witness of contemplation is, we may think of a wedding custom still observed in Iran today.

The bridegroom stands a little to one side of a mirror, so that he sees the bride enter the ceremonial room in its reflection. Likewise, the mystic never sees the divine Being directly. In the shâhid, the beautiful person to whom he gives his love, what he sees is the Image in which the divine Being contemplates himself; the shâhid is the mirror of that contemplation. Such a vision presupposes the transformation Ruzbihan describes.

At this summit, human love marks the end of divine jealousy and of the blindness of the world “without eyes”—jealousy and blindness being two sides of the same condition (see chapter III above). Ruzbihan's words are as beautiful as they are exact. They are not words one can summarize.
“There are three kinds of vision among contemplatives capable of seeing:

The first precedes earthly existence. It was the vision enjoyed by the Spirits before they entered material bodies, when they stood in the Presence of Glory. Gathering them together with the leaders of the Spirits (Ro’âsâ-e arvâh), that Presence asked them: Am I not your Lord (A-lasto bi-rabbikom, 7:171)? And with one voice they answered: Yes! The delight of those words entered their very being. They asked God for beauty, so that mystical knowledge might reach its highest perfection. Then God lifted the veil of the Jabarût, the realm of divine power, and the majestic beauty of the divine Essence appeared to them. The Spirits of the prophets and of the Friends of God (Awliyâ’) were overwhelmed by the intoxication of sacred listening and majestic beauty. They fell in love with the Eternal Witness of Contemplation (shâhid-e qidam), free from the limitations of created existence. Thus walâyat, their spiritual intimacy with God, grows in them little by little through God's schooling in love. For when the holy Spirits entered earthly bodies, their passion, which had existed before this new condition of being, made them all cry out: Show yourself to me! And each in turn found the place of exaltation, the mystical Sinai. That is why everything they saw in this world they saw as Him, so much so that one of those especially faithful to love (khowass-e mahabbat) declared: ‘There is nothing upon which I set my eyes without seeing God in it.’

Of all those who, carried away by spiritual emotion, spoke in startling paradoxes and extravagant utterances (shattâhân), not one failed to long for the sight of God or to claim to have seen him. At their gatherings, all repeated in the same language of love: I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms. As they passed through the mystical stages, all experienced the second form of love through the second kind of vision. For after passing through the initiatory trial of the veil of human existence, a person whose spiritual substance is no longer hidden by the accidents of that condition, and whose spirit overcomes the violence of physical nature, rediscovers here on earth the Original Witness of Contemplation (shâhid-e awwal). Created existence no longer disturbs him, for love has been added to love.

The third kind of vision is the highest. It takes place in the palace of mystical abiding beyond self-annihilation (baqâ’). When body and spirit have become harmonious with one another, love reaches its summit. Love grows with vision, and in the mystic it never ceases to grow, because there is no limit to the vision of the beloved. Yet among those faithful to love, the relation works the other way round: vision grows according to the degree of love. The vision of ordinary people is one thing ... The vision of those faithful to love is another ... From this you will understand that the capacity to find is proportionate to the heart. Not just anyone who tastes love's leftovers is a knight of love. For those personally initiated into love (khâssân), love is a gift bestowed upon them individually. Only then comes the vision of beauty. This station of vision has its stages, and love corresponds to the height of each stage. Love begins with the vision of grace and beauty. In the vision of supreme sublimity it ceases. When, in the state of union, a created being is invested with a lordly condition (robbânî), every divine Attribute that stirs love brings it another love to experience. If you reach this point, you will understand the teaching. Love is the shaking of one's whole being, the impetuous surging of the Spirit, the melting of the heart's innermost depths. As for the sweetness of finding, the roles of lover and beloved answer one another. It is for the beloved to awaken burning desire; for Majnun to be the man possessed by longing. Majnun's state (jonûn: enthousiasis, mania—rapture, frenzy, possession): that is love. And Majnun comes at last to be himself the mirror of God (A’yûna-e Haqq), for God makes anyone who looks into that mirror fall in love. Read this verse: He will bring forth love for them (19:96). And understand the interpretation of this one: I have cast upon you a love that comes from me (20:39).”
